speaker: periodista
text: Good afternoon and welcome to our press conference with President Lagarde and Vice President de Guindos.

speaker: periodista
text: My name is Wolfgang Preussl. As always, we are also joined by journalists who are connected via video.

speaker: periodista
text: When I give them the floor, they should please unmute and put on their camera.

speaker: periodista
text: And with that, I hand over to you, President Lagarde, please.

speaker: presidenta
text: Thank you very much, Wolfgang, and good morning, afternoon, good day to all of you. The Vice President and I welcome you to our press conference.

speaker: presidenta
text: The Governing Council today decided to keep the three key ECB interest rates unchanged.

speaker: presidenta
text: While the incoming information has been broadly consistent with our previous assessment of

speaker: presidenta
text: the inflation outlook, the upside risks to inflation and the downside risks to growth

speaker: presidenta
text: have intensified. We are committed to setting monetary policy to ensure that inflation stabilizes

speaker: presidenta
text: at our 2 percent target in the medium term. The war in the Middle East has led to a sharp

speaker: presidenta
text: increase in energy prices, pushing up inflation, and weighing on economic sentiment.

speaker: presidenta
text: The implications of the war for medium-term inflation and economic activity will depend

speaker: presidenta
text: on the intensity, the duration of the energy price shock, and the scale of its indirect

speaker: presidenta
text: and second-round effects.

speaker: presidenta
text: The longer the war continues and the longer energy prices remain high, the stronger is

speaker: presidenta
text: the likely impact on broader inflation and the economy.

speaker: presidenta
text: We remain well positioned to navigate the current uncertainty.

speaker: presidenta
text: The euro area entered this period of surging energy prices with inflation at around our

speaker: presidenta
text: 2% target and the economy has shown resilience over recent quarters. Longer-term inflation

speaker: presidenta
text: expectations remain well anchored, although inflation expectations over shorter horizons

speaker: presidenta
text: have moved up significantly. We will closely monitor the situation and follow a data-dependent

speaker: presidenta
text: and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary policy stance.

speaker: presidenta
text: In particular, our interest rate decisions will be based on our assessment of the inflation

speaker: presidenta
text: outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data,

speaker: presidenta
text: as well as the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are not pre-committing to a particular rate path.

speaker: presidenta
text: The decisions taken today are set out in a press release that is available on our website.

speaker: presidenta
text: And I will now outline in more details how we see the economy and inflation developing

speaker: presidenta
text: and will then explain our assessment of financial and monetary conditions.

speaker: presidenta
text: The euro area economy was showing some momentum when the current turbulence started.

speaker: presidenta
text: Real GDP grew by 0.1 percent in the first quarter of 26, according to Eurostat's preliminary

speaker: presidenta
text: flash estimate.

speaker: presidenta
text: Domestic demand remains the main driver of growth, supported by a resilient labor market.

speaker: presidenta
text: However, the economic outlook is highly uncertain and will depend on how long the war in the

speaker: presidenta
text: Middle East lasts, and how strongly it affects energy and other commodity markets, as well

speaker: presidenta
text: as global supply chains.

speaker: presidenta
text: The incoming information suggests that the conflict is weighing on economic activity.

speaker: presidenta
text: Surveys point to slowing growth, and consumers and businesses have become less confident

speaker: presidenta
text: about the future since the war began.

speaker: presidenta
text: delivery times and rising input prices suggest supply chains are coming under pressure.

speaker: presidenta
text: Looking ahead, high energy costs are expected to continue to weigh on real incomes, making

speaker: presidenta
text: households and firms more reluctant to consume and invest.

speaker: presidenta
text: While unemployment remained close to historical lows in March at 6.2 percent, labour demand

speaker: presidenta
text: has cooled further.

speaker: presidenta
text: At the same time, households are still benefiting from a solid financial position, and investment

speaker: presidenta
text: should continue to be underpinned by governments spending more on defence and infrastructure,

speaker: presidenta
text: and by firms increasingly investing in new digital technologies.

speaker: presidenta
text: This favorable starting point provides some cushioning against the fallout from the war.

speaker: presidenta
text: The Governing Council highlights the urgent need to strengthen the euro-area economy

speaker: presidenta
text: while maintaining sound public finances.

speaker: presidenta
text: Responsorial responses to the energy price shock should be temporary, targeted and tailored.

speaker: presidenta
text: Reforms to enhance the euro area's growth potential and accelerate the energy transition

speaker: presidenta
text: to reduce reliance on fossil fuels are more vital than ever.

speaker: presidenta
text: Completing the savings and investment union is key to funding innovation, supporting the

speaker: presidenta
text: green and digital transitions, and improving productivity.

speaker: presidenta
text: The digital euro and tokenized wholesale central bank money will enhance Europe's strategic

speaker: presidenta
text: autonomy, competitiveness and financial integration, and will boost innovation in payments.

speaker: presidenta
text: It is thus essential to swiftly adopt the regulation on the establishment of the digital

speaker: presidenta
text: euro.

speaker: presidenta
text: Simplifying and harmonizing rules across the EU's single market will help European firms

speaker: presidenta
text: grow faster.

speaker: presidenta
text: Inflation rose to 3% in April, from 2.6% in March and 1.9% in February.

speaker: presidenta
text: The rise has been driven by surging energy prices caused by the war in the Middle East.

speaker: presidenta
text: Energy price inflation jumped to 10.9% in April after 5.1% in March.

speaker: presidenta
text: Food price inflation edged up to 2.5% in April.

speaker: presidenta
text: Inflation excluding energy and food decreased to 2.2% from 2.3% in March, reflecting a fall

speaker: presidenta
text: in services.

speaker: presidenta
text: which declined to 3%, services inflation, which declined to 3% from 3.2% in March.

speaker: presidenta
text: Goods inflation went up to 0.8% from 0.5% in March.

speaker: presidenta
text: Indicators of underlying inflation have changed little over recent months.

speaker: presidenta
text: For now, the ECB's wage tracker and surveys on wage expectations continue to indicate

speaker: presidenta
text: easing labour costs in the course of 26.

speaker: presidenta
text: At the same time, surveys indicate an increase in other cost components and in selling price

speaker: presidenta
text: expectations.

speaker: presidenta
text: Inflation expectations have moved up significantly over shorter horizons.

speaker: presidenta
text: Most measures of longer-term inflation expectations stand at around 2%, supporting the stabilization

speaker: presidenta
text: of inflation around target in the medium term.

speaker: presidenta
text: The increase in energy prices will keep inflation well above 2% in the near term.

speaker: presidenta
text: As the period of high energy prices extends, the likely impact on broader inflation through

speaker: presidenta
text: indirect and second-round effects intensifies.

speaker: presidenta
text: We will therefore closely monitor the size and persistence

speaker: presidenta
text: of the energy price surge and how it feeds through to price

speaker: presidenta
text: and wage setting, inflation expectations,

speaker: presidenta
text: and overall economic dynamics.

speaker: presidenta
text: The risks to the growth outlook are to the downside.

speaker: presidenta
text: The war in the Middle East remains a downside risk

speaker: presidenta
text: to the euro-area economy,

speaker: presidenta
text: adding to the volatile global policy environment.

speaker: presidenta
text: Prolonged disruption of the supply of energy

speaker: presidenta
text: could increase energy prices further

speaker: presidenta
text: and for longer than currently expected.

speaker: presidenta
text: These factors would erode incomes

speaker: presidenta
text: and make firms and households more reluctant

speaker: presidenta
text: to invest and spend.

speaker: presidenta
text: The drag on growth would intensify if the closure of major shipping routes were to cause acute shortages of key inputs that forced euro area firms to curtail output.

speaker: presidenta
text: A worsening of global financial market sentiment could further dampen demand.

speaker: presidenta
text: National frictions in international trade could exacerbate supply chain disruptions,

speaker: presidenta
text: reduce exports, and weaken consumption and investment.

speaker: presidenta
text: Other geopolitical tensions, in particular Russia's unjustified war against Ukraine,

speaker: presidenta
text: remain a major source of uncertainty.

speaker: presidenta
text: By contrast, growth could turn out to be higher if the economy proved to be more adaptable

speaker: presidenta
text: to the disruption caused by the war in the Middle East, or if the conflict were resolved

speaker: presidenta
text: more quickly than currently expected. Moreover, planned defense and infrastructure

speaker: presidenta
text: spending reforms to enhance productivity, Euro-area firms adopting new technologies

speaker: presidenta
text: may drive up growth by more than expected. New trade agreements and a deeper integration

speaker: presidenta
text: of the single market could also boost growth beyond current expectations.

speaker: presidenta
text: The risks to the inflation outlook are to the upside.

speaker: presidenta
text: If energy prices were to rise by more and for longer than currently expected, euro area

speaker: presidenta
text: inflation would increase further.

speaker: presidenta
text: This could be reinforced and become more persistent if higher energy prices were to spill over

speaker: presidenta
text: by more than expected to other prices and to wages, if longer-term inflation expectations

speaker: presidenta
text: were to rise in response, or if global supply chains were disrupted more broadly.

speaker: presidenta
text: Ongoing trade tensions could also give rise to more fragmented global supply chains, curtail

speaker: presidenta
text: the supply of critical raw materials and worsen capacity constraints in the euro-area economy.

speaker: presidenta
text: By contrast, inflation could turn out to be lower if the economic effects of the war in

speaker: presidenta
text: the Middle East proved to be more short-lived than currently expected, or if indirect and

speaker: presidenta
text: second-round effects proved less pronounced.

speaker: presidenta
text: volatile and risk-averse financial markets could weigh on demand and thereby lower inflation

speaker: presidenta
text: as well.

speaker: presidenta
text: The war in the Middle East has caused significant volatility in global financial markets.

speaker: presidenta
text: Overall, financial conditions remain tighter than before the war.

speaker: presidenta
text: The cost of issuing market-based debt rose to 3.9% in March, from 3.5% in February.

speaker: presidenta
text: Bank lending rates to firms, based on data recorded prior to the war, edged down to 3.5%

speaker: presidenta
text: in February, while mortgage rates remained at 3.4%.

speaker: presidenta
text: The annual growth rate of bank lending to firms increased to 3.2% in March from 3% in

speaker: presidenta
text: February, while the growth rate of corporate bond issuance fell to 3.9% from 4.5% in February.

speaker: presidenta
text: Credit standards for loans to firms tightened in the first quarter, as reported in our latest

speaker: presidenta
text: bank lending survey for the euro area.

speaker: presidenta
text: This tightening was due to banks becoming more concerned about the economic risks faced

speaker: presidenta
text: by their customers.

speaker: presidenta
text: Demand for loans to firms decreased slightly in the first quarter, especially for fixed

speaker: presidenta
text: investment.

speaker: presidenta
text: Mortgage lending grew by 3% in March, after 3.1% in February, amid a small tightening

speaker: presidenta
text: in credit standards and unchanged demand.

speaker: presidenta
text: So in conclusion, the Governing Council today decided to keep the three key ECB interest

speaker: presidenta
text: rates unchanged.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are committed to setting monetary policy to ensure that inflation stabilizes at our

speaker: presidenta
text: 2% target in the medium term.

speaker: presidenta
text: We will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary

speaker: presidenta
text: policy stance. Our interest rate decisions will be based on our assessment of the inflation

speaker: presidenta
text: outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data,

speaker: presidenta
text: as well as the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are not pre-committing to a particular rate path. In any case, we stand ready to

speaker: presidenta
text: adjust all of our instruments within our mandate to ensure that inflation stabilizes sustainably

speaker: presidenta
text: at our medium-term target and to preserve the smooth functioning of monetary policy transmission.

speaker: presidenta
text: And we are now ready to take your questions. And the first question goes to Mark Schroes

speaker: periodista
text: of Bloomberg. Mark, please. Yes, thank you. President Lagarde,

speaker: periodista
text: The statement says that the upside risks to inflation and the downside risks to growth have intensified.

speaker: periodista
text: Where does this leave the ECB, this new risk assessment, leave the ECB between its baseline, its adverse and the severe scenario?

speaker: periodista
text: And what does it mean for monetary policy ahead?

speaker: periodista
text: And related to that, would you say that a rate hike in June, as expected by markets and most economists,

speaker: periodista
text: is indeed the most likely outcome unless there is a quick end to the wall and energy prices fall back quickly and significantly?

speaker: periodista
text: Thank you.

speaker: presidenta
text: I think we would all wish that there was a quick end to the war.

speaker: presidenta
text: But looking at our monetary policy and the decision that we made today, we decided to

speaker: presidenta
text: keep the three interest rates unchanged.

speaker: presidenta
text: And to address your question, I'm not going to tell you whether we are closer to the baseline

speaker: presidenta
text: scenario one, scenario two, because I think that what we have debated over the course

speaker: presidenta
text: of yesterday and today with the governing council is where are we relative to the baseline?

speaker: presidenta
text: And the conclusion is that we are certainly moving away from the baseline.

speaker: presidenta
text: Where to exactly, at what point in between baseline and other scenarios, is, I'm not

speaker: presidenta
text: sure, the most relevant assessment.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are moving away from the baseline.

speaker: presidenta
text: And what is critically important is the impact that energy prices will have.

speaker: presidenta
text: I said last time in March that it would be a question of the duration, the depth, and

speaker: presidenta
text: the propagation, and this is clearly what we need to better assess.

speaker: presidenta
text: If I was to summarize for you what we decided today, I would say that we made an informed

speaker: presidenta
text: decision on the basis of yet insufficient information.

speaker: presidenta
text: So why do I say it's an informed decision?

speaker: presidenta
text: It's because we debated at length and in depth various options.

speaker: presidenta
text: We debated the decision that we have unanimously taken today, but we also debated at length

speaker: presidenta
text: and in depth a decision to possibly hike.

speaker: presidenta
text: So that was debated amongst all governors, and I'm sure that you will meet some governors

speaker: presidenta
text: who will argue both sides, or maybe one side, of both proposals.

speaker: presidenta
text: So it was really a deeply discussed monetary policy stance, of which the outcome was a

speaker: presidenta
text: a unanimous decision to leave the three interest rates unchanged.

speaker: presidenta
text: And I'm saying that it's an informed decision based on insufficient information.

speaker: presidenta
text: It is caused by the fact that while the hard data is broadly in line with our projection

speaker: presidenta
text: and what we discussed here back in March.

speaker: presidenta
text: But there is such uncertainty that we

speaker: presidenta
text: need to understand and revisit all of that

speaker: presidenta
text: at our next monetary policy meeting.

speaker: presidenta
text: And we believe that given the position we are in,

speaker: presidenta
text: we are saying in the monetary policy statement

speaker: presidenta
text: that we started from a good position.

speaker: presidenta
text: We were well positioned to navigate.

speaker: presidenta
text: So given that position, we believe that these six weeks

speaker: presidenta
text: will be the right time to assess the development,

speaker: presidenta
text: to understand in particular the outcome, possibly,

speaker: presidenta
text: of the conflict, or if there is no outcome,

speaker: presidenta
text: that in and of itself will be informative,

speaker: presidenta
text: in order to make an informed decision

speaker: presidenta
text: on verified and revisited information

speaker: presidenta
text: that we will receive in the next six months.

speaker: presidenta
text: That's the clearest way, I hope it was clear,

speaker: presidenta
text: that I can describe for the really good discussions

speaker: presidenta
text: that we had both yesterday and today.

speaker: periodista
text: Next question to Annette Weisbach of CNBC.

speaker: periodista
text: Annette, please.

speaker: vicepresidente
text: President Lagarde, thank you for taking my questions.

speaker: vicepresidente
text: I have a question on whether you have also discussed

speaker: vicepresidente
text: that the risk of a stagflationary scenario

speaker: vicepresidente
text: on the euro area and how that discussion went.

speaker: vicepresidente
text: And also, in the US, they are starting

speaker: vicepresidente
text: to also think about shrinking the balance sheet

speaker: vicepresidente
text: instead of using interest rate as a monetary policy instrument.

speaker: vicepresidente
text: Do you look into using other instruments as well,

speaker: vicepresidente
text: instead of just hiking, to alleviate the pressure

speaker: vicepresidente
text: from the price pressure and also help, perhaps, the economy?

speaker: vicepresidente
text: Thank you.

speaker: presidenta
text: Well, thank you for your two questions.

speaker: presidenta
text: On the first one,

speaker: presidenta
text: you know, we take the view that the word,

speaker: presidenta
text: I mean, it's quite popular to talk about stagflation,

speaker: presidenta
text: and it flags a lot of anxiety and all the rest of it.

speaker: presidenta
text: I think we have determined that stagflation

speaker: presidenta
text: is the right characterization of what happened in the 70s.

speaker: presidenta
text: But from our perspective, we think that it's better to park it in the 70s,

speaker: presidenta
text: given the facts that we have at the moment.

speaker: presidenta
text: You know, it's a completely different situation.

speaker: presidenta
text: In the 70s, you had inflation continuing, continuing, continuing,

speaker: presidenta
text: at a, you know, sort of sustainable and solid pace.

speaker: presidenta
text: You had very high unemployment.

speaker: presidenta
text: You had a monetary and fiscal framework that had nothing to do with what we have at the moment. So we don't apply stagflation, that flashy term, to the circumstances that we have

speaker: presidenta
text: because we really think that it's associated with the 70s situation.

speaker: presidenta
text: On the tools, we have a whole series of tools in our toolbox.

speaker: presidenta
text: But certainly from our perspective, and given the data that we have and the kind of shock that we're facing,

speaker: presidenta
text: We believe that the interest rates is still the best tool that we can use

speaker: presidenta
text: and that we have debated in the course of yesterday and today.

speaker: presidenta
text: Thank you.

speaker: periodista
text: Francesco Canepa of Reuters. Francesco, please.

speaker: periodista
text: Thank you very much.

speaker: periodista
text: So, first question about your reaction function.

speaker: periodista
text: Could you unpack a little the relative weight that you attach to growth and inflation in your reaction function?

speaker: periodista
text: and second about the scenarios did you update them and if so what do they look like now and why if i may do you not think it relevant to to say where we are now compared to the

speaker: periodista
text: compared to the baseline and the two scenarios thanks

speaker: presidenta
text: i'm so pleased that you mentioned the reaction function

speaker: presidenta
text: because it's, you know, we spend quite a lot of time working it out,

speaker: presidenta
text: finding consensus around the reaction function.

speaker: presidenta
text: And as you know, because you're a frequent reader and observers of what we do,

speaker: presidenta
text: the reaction function has been very clearly spelt out

speaker: presidenta
text: in our strategy review that we published in 25

speaker: presidenta
text: and that I have tried to elaborate on

speaker: presidenta
text: and that I have tried to apply to the current circumstances

speaker: presidenta
text: in both my speech to the Watchers

speaker: presidenta
text: and my speech in Berlin last week.

speaker: presidenta
text: So I think, for me, there are sort of three...

speaker: presidenta
text: We love to work with three because it's pillars.

speaker: presidenta
text: But I have for myself three anchors

speaker: presidenta
text: of what our reaction function is.

speaker: presidenta
text: So first of all, to remind you,

speaker: presidenta
text: target is 2% medium term, number one.

speaker: presidenta
text: Number two, symmetry.

speaker: presidenta
text: We discussed that today, and we reaffirmed it.

speaker: presidenta
text: Number three, our reaction will depend on the type of deviation from target that we observe.

speaker: presidenta
text: Is it large and sustainable?

speaker: presidenta
text: In that case, obviously, we have calibrated in our strategy review and in those two speeches that I have committed in the last few days,

speaker: presidenta
text: in that case, we have a forceful or persistent reaction

speaker: presidenta
text: to return inflation to our target of 2% medium term.

speaker: presidenta
text: That's our reaction function.

speaker: presidenta
text: And the data and the process that we use

speaker: presidenta
text: in order to deliver on that reaction function

speaker: presidenta
text: is what you see, monetary policy statement

speaker: presidenta
text: after monetary policy statement,

speaker: presidenta
text: which is the inflation outlook with the risks associated

speaker: presidenta
text: to it. And as you will have seen in the MPS, we have a strong chapter on both risks to growth and

speaker: presidenta
text: risk to inflation. That's how we bring in the risk to growth, to your point. We also look at

speaker: presidenta
text: underlying inflation, and we look at the dynamics of monetary policy transmission. So the reaction

speaker: presidenta
text: function, the process and the tools that we use in order to apply that reaction function. And of

speaker: presidenta
text: And of course we look at the specificity of what we are going through and that's where

speaker: presidenta
text: you will find more details in both my speech to the watchers, you are one of them I'm sure,

speaker: presidenta
text: and my speech in Berlin to the bankers.

speaker: presidenta
text: And I think I tried in those two documents, particularly the latter, to really apply the

speaker: presidenta
text: the reaction function and the tools

speaker: presidenta
text: to the circumstances through which we're going,

speaker: presidenta
text: in particular, a supply shock, a strong supply shock,

speaker: presidenta
text: negative one, of course,

speaker: presidenta
text: and to see whether we are going to use one or the other

speaker: presidenta
text: or the other approaches, approach,

speaker: presidenta
text: in order to deliver on our target of 2% medium term.

speaker: presidenta
text: And one is see-through.

speaker: presidenta
text: Anyway, I don't need to repeat my Berlin speech.

speaker: presidenta
text: It's, some of you have read it.

speaker: presidenta
text: Oh yeah, you asked me about the scenarios.

speaker: presidenta
text: So,

speaker: presidenta
text: we constantly monitor.

speaker: presidenta
text: We constantly take in new data, hard data, soft data,

speaker: presidenta
text: survey results from all sorts of perspectives

speaker: presidenta
text: and we verify and we adjust

speaker: presidenta
text: And we take stock of all that.

speaker: presidenta
text: In June, six weeks from now, you will be receiving

speaker: presidenta
text: not only the projections that our staff will produce,

speaker: presidenta
text: but you will also see the scenarios as revised

speaker: presidenta
text: and as updated as a result of the circumstances.

speaker: periodista
text: Turning now to the participants via video link,

speaker: periodista
text: I'd like to give the floor to Isabella Bouffaki

speaker: periodista
text: of 24, no, il solo 24 ore. Isabella, please. Thank you for the opportunity. I have two
questions on liquidity, which is key to the implementation of monetary policy, but also
crucial for financial stability in times of crisis like we have now. So, President Lagarde,
euro area central bank reserves have almost halved from the peak in 2022 to 2.6 trillion
in early 2026. And in the last bank lending survey, we found out that the bank access to
money market funding has deteriorated. So has the governing council been looking at the design of
new liquidity tools, as you had a question before on your toolbox, new liquidity tools in the
operational framework, for example, new structural longer-term credit operations or structural
portfolio of securities. And my second question is for Vice President Luis de Guindos. At the end
of your eight-year mandate and eight years of multiple crises, what is your assessment of the
resilience of the banking systems in terms of liquidity? And what about private credit players
that do not have access to the ECB liquidity? Is all this enough? Thank you.

speaker: presidenta
text: Well, thank you so much. We miss you here, but it's nice to see you.

speaker: presidenta
text: So I'll take the first question, and then I'll give the floor to the vice president.

speaker: presidenta
text: We still have abundance of liquidity.

speaker: presidenta
text: You mentioned 2.6. I think it's a little down from that number, but it's a significant amount of excess liquidity in the system.

speaker: presidenta
text: So there is no shortage of liquidity.

speaker: presidenta
text: And as you know, we have a mechanism that works on the basis of access to liquidity.

speaker: presidenta
text: You know, it's a fixed interest rate, full allotment, good collaterals.

speaker: presidenta
text: It's working well, and we're not seeing any tension in that respect.

speaker: presidenta
text: Did we discuss new tools?

speaker: presidenta
text: The answer is no, because what we discussed, and it was on the agenda yesterday, We discussed the timetable and the methodology that will be adopted in-house by staff as well as within the euro system, bringing all the committees in the loop to calibrate our operational framework to make sure that it is fit for purpose and that it is good from a financial stability point of view as well as from a proper functioning of the providing of liquidity,

speaker: presidenta
text: which is obviously one of the missions that we have.

speaker: presidenta
text: With that, I'll turn the floor over to you, my dear Luis.
Thank you very much, President.
Good afternoon to everyone.
Well, we have no doubts about the liquidity position
and the capital position of the European banks.
The European banks are resilient,
and we do not believe that liquidity or capital
is any sort of limitation for lending.
And this is something that we have analysed quite in detail.

So, I would say that we are confident that they have enough liquidity, that they have enough capital, and that they are meeting the purpose that we want to deliver, that is, that banks meet the needs and the financial needs of families, households and corporates.
You referred to private credit.
Well, we are going to dedicate a full chapter of our financial stability review to private credit. It's something that is catching the eye of markets because of some liquidity issues.
Private credit is a totally different animal in comparison with the banks in terms of oversight,
in terms of the way that they function.
and we are going to analyse interlinkages between private credit and other players as insurance companies,
as the banks, and with private equity. And I think that you will have a full explanation of our approach
and our assessment of the potential financial stability risks posed by the private credit
in our financial stability review that is going to be published in three weeks.

speaker: periodista
text: Next question goes to Olaf Steuberg with the Financial Times.

speaker: periodista
text: Olaf, please.
Thanks for taking my questions.
My first question is on a scenario that some economists discuss at the moment,
which is basically a return to the 2011 scenario,
where the ECB hiked relatively early on,
